speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We last undertook an extensive review of the Penal Code in 2018 and 2019, and amendments were made in 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That included amendments to strengthen the protection for minors and other vulnerable victims; deal with new crime trends; better deal with sexual offences; expand and clarify the scope of certain offences and defences; and modernise the language of certain provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will speak on some of the amendments relating to sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleague, Minister of State Desmond Tan, will take the House through the amendments in greater detail.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As this House is aware, we have made significant changes in legislation over the years, to deal with sexual crimes and strengthen the protection for women, children and vulnerable persons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are set out in the Annex to my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And Sir, with your permission, can I ask the Clerk to distribute the Annex to Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can also access this information, this material through the Singapore Parliament Members of Parliament mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In particular, we made several key changes to the Penal Code in 2019.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will highlight a few as relevant background for this Bill before I deal with this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sexual activity with this category of minors was criminalised where the relationship was exploitative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These minors above the age of 16 are slightly above the age of consent for sexual activity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can consent but in reality, they are susceptible to exploitation by those who are in a relationship of trust with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In such cases, the minor's consent is compromised and we dealt with that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, we introduced for the offence of procuring sexual activity by deception or false representation to deal with cases where the victim's consent was compromised due to the offender misleading them on the use of, for example, sexually protective measures or the absence of a sexually transmitted disease.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This sought to protect victims from violations to their sexual autonomy and the serious risks that arise from that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fifth, we specifically made voyeurism an offence to address technology-facilitated offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Previously, such offences would be dealt with under the rubric of insulting the modesty of a woman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The new offence of voyeurism doubled the maximum imprisonment term from one to two years and provided for the possibility of caning as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the Bill before the House today, we also deal with sexual offences, amongst other matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I stated in my Ministerial Statement in March, the maximum penalties are in our view properly calibrated for most of the offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are, however, three sexual offences for which we intend to increase the maximum punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, on outrage of modesty (OM) under section 354(1) of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have seen an increased in the number of OM cases from 2016 to 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had an average of 1,190 cases reported each year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will enhance deterrence and ensure that egregious cases are punished more severely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This maximum imprisonment term of three years is only for the primary offence of OM under section 354(1).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are other aggravated variants of the offence such as OM against minors under 14 or where hurt is caused to the victim in order to commit OM, which already attract higher penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, we will raise the penalties for sexual offences against minors for two sexual offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the offence under section 376ED(3)(b) of engaging in sexual activity in the presence of a minor between 14 and 16 years of age or causing a minor between 14 and 16 years of age to view a sexual image; Second, the offence under section 376EE(3), which prohibits the same conduct against a minor between 16 and 18 years of age where the offender is in an exploitative relationship with the minor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An exploitative relationship may be found, for example, between a parent or a step-parent, teacher, sports coach, musical instructor of the minor and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Currently, the maximum imprisonment term for these two offences is one year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will bring the punishment in line with similar offences involving sexual communications with minors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Apart from increasing the penalties for these three offences, the Bill also makes amendments to other sexual offences such as sexual assault involving penetration, procuring sexual activity by deception or false representation, sexual penetration of a corpse, offences relating to voyeurism and intimate images, and offences relating to child abuse material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These amendments will clarify the scope of the offences and finetune them further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister of State Desmond Tan will take the House through other amendments in his speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Minister Shanmugam has spoken on the amendments relating to the increased penalties for three sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In my speech, I will explain how this Bill expands and clarifies the scope of certain offences and defences, and modernises the language of certain provisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, one gap that the Bill is meant to address is the giving of false information to public servants in the course of their duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The need to review this arises from a recent decision of the High Court, Public Prosecutor v Chua Wen Hao.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In that case, the Police were looking for a suspect who had committed an offence at a hotel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At the hotel, the Police asked the accused person whether he knew the suspect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The accused person told the Police that he did not and that he had not allowed such a person to enter his hotel room.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Police investigations subsequently revealed that this was not true.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In fact, not only was the accused person a friend of the suspect, they had gone out for drinks together and had planned to meet at the hotel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The suspect arrived at the hotel slightly after the accused person and joined him in his hotel room.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As a result of the false information, Police officers wasted additional effort and time to uncover the identity of the suspect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The accused person was charged under section 182 of the Penal Code, which provides for the offence of giving false information to a public servant with the intent of causing or knowing that it will likely cause a public servant to use his lawful power to the injury or annoyance of another person or to do or omit anything which the public servant ought not to do or omit if he had known the truth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The High Court held that section 182 did not apply as the offence is concerned with situations where the offender intends to cause or knows that he will likely cause a public servant to abuse, misuse or improperly withhold the use of his or her lawful powers as a result of the false information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The High Court held that the offence does not cover cases where a person gives false information with the intent of causing or knowing that it will likely cause the public servant to be ineffective and inefficient in exercising his lawful powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Giving false information to a public servant who is carrying out his or her duties is a very serious matter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There can be very serious consequences, for example, when the Police are hunting for a suspect in a murder or sexual assault case or when SCDF officers are responding to an emergency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The delay in identifying the offender could be a matter of life and death.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This would cover cases where the false information results in the inefficient exercise of the public servant's lawful powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In addition, clause 13 amends section 186 of the Penal Code, which criminalises the voluntary obstruction of a public servant in the discharge of his or her public functions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Whether the false information does in fact amount to obstruction is a question of fact for the Court to determine in each case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These amendments will strengthen our levers to deal with offenders who deceive public servants and in so doing, harm public interests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Turning to the other offences, first, clause 23 amends section 376 of the Penal Code, which provides for the offence of sexual assault involving penetration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Subsection (1) of section 376 makes it an offence for a male offender to cause a male victim to penetrate the offender's anus or mouth with the victim's penis without the victim's consent or where the victim is below 14 years of age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This subsection will be deleted as the conduct is already covered under the broader subsection (2)(b).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, the offence of sexual assault involving penetration is gender-neutral.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It can be committed by males or females.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Therefore, we will also amend the defence under section 376(6) so that both male and female offenders may rely on it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, clause 28 amends section 376H of the Penal Code, which makes it an offence for a person to procure consent to sexual activity by deception or false representation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The offence will also be widened to cover cases where the offender deceives the victim into consenting to being touched by a third person or into touching the bodily fluids of the offender or another person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 29 amends the offence of sexual penetration of a corpse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The offence currently prohibits a man from penetrating a corpse's vagina, anus or mouth with his penis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It also prohibits any person from causing a man to do so without the man's consent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The proposed amendments will (a) criminalise other forms of sexual penetration involving corpses; and (b) make the offender gender-neutral.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 30 broadens the scope of the offence of voyeurism under section 377BB by replacing the term "genitals" with "genital region".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This will ensure that the offence is wide enough to cover cases where the offender manages to capture an image of the victim's genital region but not the genitals themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clauses 31 and 34 deal with the definitions of "child abuse material" and "abusive material" under section 377C and section 377BL.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This will enhance protections for minors by ensuring that the relevant offences apply to sexual images of scantily-clad children or close-up images of the child's genitals, buttocks or breasts – even if covered by clothing – in circumstances which reasonable persons would regard as offensive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In addition, the Bill clarifies that the depictions must be sexual in nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This will make clear that the intent is not to cover non-sexual depictions of minors, such as diaper advertisements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, under section 512 of the Penal Code, a person who attempts to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment will face a maximum imprisonment term of 20 years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, where a person abets the commission of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment but that offence is ultimately not committed, section 115 only provides a maximum imprisonment term of 15 years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is even though an abettor under section 115 may be equally culpable as or even more culpable than a person who attempts to commit such an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I now turn to the amendments relating to the operation of certain defences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clauses 5, 6 and 7 amend the provisions relating to mistake or ignorance of fact, mistake or ignorance of law and accident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These clauses are intended to provide greater clarity on the way these provisions operate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They do not change the general common law principles on burden of proof, namely, that the prosecution must prove the elements of the offence and that the accused person must prove a defence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, clauses 8, 9 and 17 amend the defence of unsoundness of mind, the defence of intoxication and the partial defence of diminished responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The amendments clarify that where an accused person claims that he was incapable of knowing that what he was doing wrong, by reason of unsoundness of mind, the accused person must prove that he was incapable of knowing that what he was doing was both wrong by the ordinary standards of reasonable and honest persons, and wrong as contrary to law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In other words, the two limbs are to be read conjunctively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This was in fact the position taken when the Penal Code was last amended in 2019, where we inserted the illustration to section 84.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The present amendments only serve to make this clearer and do not change the state of the current law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If criminal force was used on grave and sudden provocation, a less serious offence under section 358 will apply instead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Currently, the explanation under section 352 provides that the partial defence of grave and sudden provocation does not apply if, among other things, the provocation was given by anything done in obedience to the law or by a public servant in the lawful exercise of the public servant's power.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This means that an accused person cannot rely on the partial defence in this scenario, even if the accused person did not know and had no reason to believe that the provocation was given by anything done in obedience to the law or by a public servant in the lawful exercise of the public servant's power.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This aligns the partial defence of grave and sudden provocation under section 352 with the partial defence of grave and sudden provocation for more serious offences such as murder, voluntarily causing grievous hurt and voluntarily causing hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Similar amendments will be made to the partial defence of provocation where it appears in other Penal Code provisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Lastly, this Bill seeks to modernise the language of certain provisions under the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to touch on two areas in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead, we should look to whether the person is medically fit to be caned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If it is found to be so, age should be no impediment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the first point, I note that it is proposed that before an accused may rely on the defence of unsoundness of mind under section 84 of the Penal Code, he needs to prove that he is both incapable of knowing that what he did was wrong by the ordinary standards of reasonable and honest persons; and wrong as contrary to law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, he did not know what he did was both morally and legally wrong.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I further note that the amendments do not seek to widen the ambit of section 84, which covers only cognitive disorders, to include conative or volitional disorders; meaning to include situations where the accused simply cannot control his actions because of a mental disorder.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am concerned that, because of the two observations that I made, the ambit of the proposed section 84 is too narrow and this may not be in public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Any lawyer who has raised the defence of unsoundness of mind in Court, and I have done so, would know that an acquittal represents somewhat a Pyrrhic victory.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because when an accused is held to have done the offending act but acquitted on the grounds of unsoundness of mind, will be ordered by the Minister to be kept in safe custody, usually, in a psychiatric institution "during the President’s pleasure".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, he will be incarcerated at the institution indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst there, he would receive treatment and would be monitored every six months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister who gets the six-monthly reports on the accused, may order him to be discharged, if it is determined that the accused would not be a danger to himself and to others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead of narrowing the ambit of section 84 of the Penal Code, it is my respectful view that public interest may be better served with a broader section 84, so that in an appropriate case, the Court is able to invoke the provisions to ensure that a person who is suffering from a serious mental illness, gets inpatient psychiatric treatment for as long as he would be a danger to himself and the public.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As it stands today, he may be punished and sentenced in the usual way.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If he were to be sentenced to imprisonment, the public will then have to run the risk that the person may reoffend after serving the sentence, causing harm to himself or others, because of his continuing mental illness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that case, the accused, aged 55, murdered his own uncle by bludgeoning him to death with a stool.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The trial judge described the killing as "utterly gruesome".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The accused, however, was suffering from chronic schizophrenia which brought about a persecutory delusion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through his counsel, he pleaded guilty to a charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of diminished responsibility.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The accused however did not raise the defence of unsoundness of mind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It recognised that it is arguable that the accused should deserve compassion and leniency since what he did was because of his mental illness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ordinarily, this would have meant that he should be sentenced to imprisonment not exceeding 10 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That in turn, would have meant he would have been back in circulation in about seven years' time after taking into account remission.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given his mental illness, this may cause further danger to himself and others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Naturally, the Court felt that such an eventuality was not desirable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It rued over the fact that the defence of unsoundness of mind was not invoked because that would allow the accused to be kept in custody in a psychiatric institution for so long as necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, the Court, after expressing a lot of difficulty, decided to impose a life imprisonment sentence purely on a utilitarian basis, that is, of course, not doctrinally ideal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would also add that since then, we have passed in this House, provisions that would allow for the imposition of Mandatory Treatment Orders (MTOs) on persons who, as a result of their psychiatric conditions, committed minor offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some years back, I argued in this House for a widening of the ambit of offences for which MTOs may be imposed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This led to the issuance of the Criminal Procedure Code (Prescribed Offences for Mandatory Treatment Orders) Regulations 2018 which prescribed a wider list of more serious offences for which MTOs can be imposed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, the trend where persons with mental illnesses are concerned, is where possible, to impose sentences which will allow them to get treatment which will, hopefully, allow them not to continue with their harmful behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, amendments were made in this House to the text of section 84 of the Penal Code in 2019.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had occasion to review the speeches made by the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary then, who moved several Penal Code amendments, which included section 84 of the Penal Code in 2019.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, it was a missed opportunity for the Government to explain why it was taking a different tack from the PCRC which advocated a broadening of the unsound mind defence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fairness, as the hon Minister of State said, I noted the illustration too, that was introduced through the amendment of section 84 of the Penal Code which, on its own, seems to manifest an intention that a conjunctive interpretation should be adopted for the amended section 84 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am however not surprised that the current amendments are still being sought to amend the wording of section 84.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because it is specifically provided under section 7A of the Interpretation Act, where an illustration is inconsistent with the provision, the provision prevails.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, parliamentary intention could not have been sufficiently manifested by mere reference to the illustration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result of these developments, even though this provision is being amended for the second time in two years, this is probably the first time that we will be able to hear why is it that it is being proposed to narrow the ambit of section 84 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would invite the hon Minister of State to please explain why it is felt that the conjunctive interpretation is to be preferred over the disjunctive interpretation of section 84 of the Penal Code; and why is that section 84 is still not broadened to include volitional acts?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the primary intention of this Bill which is to enhance penalties for some sexual offences such as outrage of modesty, sexual activity in presence of a minor and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having regard to the crime trend that is being highlighted, I support the amendments to the sentencing provisions that will enable more deterrent sentences to be imposed in egregious cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This includes not just imprisonment but caning too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I would like to focus on in my speech is whether the provisions providing for the sentence of caning that may be imposed by the Court on male offenders for committing serious sexual offences are fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has been interpreted by the Court of Appeal in 2015 decision of Yong Vui Kong v PP, to mean that Parliament intended to use the age of 50 as "a convenient proxy to screen out those who are likely to be unfit for caning", given that there is "an inverse relationship between one's age and one's physical condition".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also highlighted that the life expectancy at birth for males in Britain, from which the Criminal Procedure Code was enacted in Singapore through Imperial legislation, was 47.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The cut-off age more or less coincided with the life expectancy of males at that time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: More than 120 years later, the life expectancy at birth for males in Singapore is slightly more than 80 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I further pointed out that in Malaysia, whilst the age of 50 has still been retained as a cut-off point for caning, when it comes to serious sexual offences, there is no cut-off age for a male convicted for a serious sexual offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So long as he is assessed to be medically fit, he can be caned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I asked if the provision limiting caning for serious sexual offenders to males below 50 is fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In reply, the hon Minister of State informed this House then, that her Ministry will look into it and take steps as necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: More than a year later, I remain concerned whether the provision is still fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also wish to highlight an unintended consequence of maintaining the age of 50 as a cut-off age.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just a few days ago on 31 August 2021, The Straits Times published an article of a case of a man who was convicted in 2001 and sentenced to 19 years' jail and 24 strokes of the cane for rape and other sexual offences committed against his then-stepdaughter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After coming out of prison in 2013, the man, after less than three years, sexually abused his two grand-nieces aged nine and 11 respectively.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The irony is that even though he is a repeat offender, he will be getting a sentence without caning because he crossed the age of 50.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This state of affairs, with respect, is not desirable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not see why Parliament should presume in his favour, in favour of a repeat sex offender, that he is not fit to be caned when he is clearly fit to commit those heinous acts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also think it is not a coincidence that such middle-aged offenders tend to target younger victims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to ensure that such like-minded offenders will be strongly deterred from harming them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I welcome the hon Minister of State’s response to the points I make about caning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, in his Second Reading speech, the Minister reiterated the Government's position as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I wish to instead raise some reservations about another aspect of the Bill: the changes to the offences involving giving false information to public servants or obstructing them in their duty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Overall, it appears to me that the changes in the Bill will result in a blurring of the distinctions between different offences and I am not clear as to why this is necessary or desirable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 12, the scope of the offence under section 182 of the Penal Code will be expanded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Section 182 deals with the offence of giving false information, with intent to cause a public servant to use his lawful power to the injury of another person.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This denial led the Police to spend nearly 22 man-hours on investigations to establish the identity of the culprit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In giving his judgment in the case, as noted by the Minister of State earlier, the Chief Justice ruled that section 182 did not cover a situation where the false information simply led to a public servant being inefficient in exercising his lawful powers to investigate the case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He ruled that section 182 was meant to cover situations where the offender intended or knew that the false information would likely lead the public servant to abuse or misuse his powers, or to improperly omit to use lawful powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such scenarios would include false statements that lead to a wrongful arrest, or which subject innocent persons to annoyance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such conduct is already caught by section 177.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the sub-heading or marginal note to section 182 is not being amended, so it will still read "False information, with intent to cause a public servant to use his lawful power to the injury of another person".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could result in some misunderstanding by the public as to the scope of the section.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It, therefore, seems to me that there will now be a blurring of the lines between sections 177 and 182, and the rationale for this change is not compelling.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet another blurring may be caused by clause 13, which amends section 186 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Section 186 deals with "Obstructing public servant in discharge of his public functions".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 13, a new subsubsection (2) will be added, to state that obstructing a public servant may be caused other than by use of physical means or threatening language.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There now appears to be yet another overlap between offences, in that giving false information could come within section 177 and also within section 186.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will the Police decide which section to charge a person under?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I support these increases in penalties to act as a greater deterrent against such offending behaviour and to allow the Courts to mete out harsher sentences for perpetrators of these offences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, we also need to look at how to ensure that victims have avenues to seek support and assistance to make Police reports if crimes are committed against them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly so for minors who are victims of such offences.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I am heartened by the various efforts made by the Government to make it easier and less straining on minor victims to describe what they had gone through.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the multi-disciplinary interview model for children who have been sexually abused by their family members consolidates interviews from various parties into just one interview, so that child victims do not need to repeat accounts of traumatic experiences multiple times.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I note also that the National Institute of Early Childhood includes in its curriculum for teachers, concepts of body safety, such as identifying good or bad touches and how to teach children protective skills to prevent sexual abuse.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, I look forward to the findings of the review on whether screening should be implemented for persons who work with children.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I turn now to seek clarification on specific clauses in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Before I go on, I declare my interest, Sir, as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My humble submission is that this does not provide sufficient clarity as what exactly is included in this new term “genital region” which could extend to the upper thigh, pelvis, pubis or lower stomach.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would urge that the Minister consider including a definition or illustrations to make clear what “genital region” refers to.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I refer to clause 12 which seeks to amend the current section 182 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: CJ Menon observed in that case that there was a distinction that had to be drawn between a "misuse" of Police powers, where an officer ought not to have done something, which is the wording of section 182 in the current Penal Code and an "inefficient" use of Police powers, that is, something the officer would not or might not have done.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This same clause and section was raised just before me by Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Would it also mean that an accused person may end up being charged for a more serious offence under section 182 instead of a lesser offence with lower penalties under section 177?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, Sir, I would like to seek updates on two matters related to today’s Bill and the wider criminal law framework.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I would like to urge the Government to commence a study of whether the identities of persons accused of sexual crimes should be published until they have been convicted and exhausted all avenues of appeal.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The recent case of Dr Yeo Sow Nam who obtained a discharge amounting to acquittal illustrates how an innocent person can have his name sullied and suffer public and long-term stigma, which affects not only his professional life, but also his personal life.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To quote Dr Yeo: "It was humiliating, a lot of ignominy, public shame, a feeling of persecution by the country I love when I have not done anything wrong".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, such crimes, because they often occur in private, tend to have a "he-said-she-said" character.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Courts themselves have acknowledged this in how they assess the evidence adduced, in requiring that testimony be "unusually convincing" for a conviction.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I also urge that the study consider whether such protection should be provided until all avenues of appeal are exhausted.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This follows from the case of Ong Ming Wee, who was convicted for rape in the first instance, but acquitted on appeal.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister for Law has addressed this matter in extent in May, in response to a Parliamentary Question by my fellow Nominated Member of Parliament colleague Dr Tan Yia Swam, in which he said that the Ministry will keep, and I quote, "under review" its current position where the accused is named at the onset of proceedings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Minister will consider a formal review and a formal consideration of the pros and cons of introducing protections for persons accused of sexual crimes and under what circumstances.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications and suggestions, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The amendments made in the Criminal Law Bill are in light of the current trends in our legal landscape.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to raise three clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must recognise that sexual offences are not only physically damaging but it scars the victims emotionally and psychologically.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There has been an alarming increase of outrage of modesty cases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the rise in cases, the harsher sentences will act as a strong deterrence for would-be offenders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The increased use of the digital space amongst our youth, unfortunately, also increases the chance of them being exposed to sexual grooming, sometimes even on seemingly innocent online platforms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond just sending inappropriate pictures and content to the vulnerable, I would like to clarify if this also includes sending hyperlinks of sexual images or hyperlinks to sexual content and websites through platforms, such as Instagram Chat, WhatsApp chat, Tik Tok comments, or chat on games platforms like Minecraft or Roblox.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, these hyperlinks are also deceptively embedded in an online chat and take the form of what is known as "clickbait".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An innocent child may inadvertently be routed to inappropriate content and this is, indeed, something that is increasingly worrying.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, what legal action can be taken by the Ministry if the perpetrators are not in Singapore as it is more than conceivable that online sexual grooming can occur across state borders?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we have the capability and resource to track such offenders if there is, indeed, one?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how do we prevent such sexual offenders from taking on roles which may put others at risk?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, will they be barred from becoming teachers or private tutors and coaches?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And what happens when a person on such an offenders’ list is successfully rehabilitated and fully repentant?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The change to gender-neutral language also reflects the unfortunate realities of such heinous acts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Any vulnerable person can be a victim and to characterise a person as a potential offender through a checklist, is creating caricatures.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, it is of utmost importance that parents and guardians be mindful about who is trustworthy, exercise vigilance and educate the young to spot and report what is not appropriate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, the community has a responsibility to create safe spaces for the vulnerable to report such acts without shame, guilt or fear.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While harsher sentences do act as a deterrence, how can we further protect the vulnerable against convicted offenders?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we enhance the protection to our children and allow parents to make an informed decision?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of our children are taking private tuition, coaching lessons, or extracurricular activities, such as piano lessons.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It can even extend to school bus drivers and their attendants, and vendors for after-school programmes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is of paramount importance that we do not make our children more vulnerable than they already are.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For convicted offenders of sexual offences who prey on victims online, can the Ministry consider monitoring their online activities during their rehabilitation period after they have served their sentences?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only after they have been suitably assessed as having been fully rehabilitated would they then be allowed to exercise the liberties of regular citizens.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These two methods may prove to be more of a deterrent to potential offenders than simply increasing the maximum sentence of the offences.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, while we support harsher sentences, we must also protect the wrongly accused.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The nature of sexual offences is such that it takes a lot courage for a victim to proceed in making a report.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Self-doubt, embarrassment and even a sense of self-blame plague many victims.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is because of this mental anguish, on top of any physical harm and abuse that have already occurred, that perpetrators must be brought to justice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, it should not be abused by the very few who, out of spite or mischief, decide to lodge such reports.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   There has been an alarming increase of outrage of modesty cases.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Between 2016 and 2020, the number of outrage of modesty cases reported was 24% higher than the number of cases from 2011 to 2015.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the rise in cases, the harsher sentences will act as a strong deterrence for would-be offenders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The increasingly widespread use of digital space amongst our youths, unfortunately, also increases the chances of them being exposed to sexual grooming, sometimes even on seemingly innocent online platforms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Parents play a role in educating the young and those who are more vulnerable by monitoring their online activities so that they do not fall prey to such acts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I suggest that parents and guardians be mindful about who is trustworthy and can be trusted and exercise vigilance and educate the young to spot and report inappropriate activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our society has a responsibility to create safe spaces for the vulnerable and to report such acts without hesitation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Certainly, it is not easy for victims of sexual offences to lodge a report.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They need to be strong and to summon their courage to make the report.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Self-doubt, shame and even a sense of self-blame plague many victims.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is because of this mental anguish on top of the physical harm that they suffer that perpetrators must be brought to justice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, our justice system must not be so onerous for victims to pursue justice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, it should not also be abused by the very few who lodge such reports in bad faith.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, allow me to conclude in English.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments in this Bill have been raised through a considered process and take into account public moral norms as seen through reactions to high-profile sentencing decisions in sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is consistent with Minister Shanmugam’s Ministerial Statement last month, when Minister stated that the sentences for sexual and hurt offences must reflect that such acts are deeply offensive to society’s fundamental values.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also in line with this is the announcement that AGC will, generally, object to rehabilitative sentences, such as probation and community-based sentences, where the offenders are adults who commit certain types of hurt or sexual offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with the strong signal sent by focusing on the punitive purpose of sentencing for adult offenders of hurt and sexual offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, even with a harsh sentence, there remains a need to ensure that such offenders receive appropriate counselling and treatment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what kinds of counselling and treatment are provided to offenders of hurt and sexual offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will they receive such treatment only during their sentence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there scope to consider mandating post-release treatment for such offenders, where medical and psychiatric professionals deem necessary?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the changes of the fault element for certain offences from “malice” to “intent to cause injury” for certain offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The purpose of this is to clarify the fault element of the offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Injury is defined under the Penal Code as “any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm that an “intent to cause injury” does not succeed in causing the specific type of injury intended, or the offender does not succeed in injuring the intended victim?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify whether emotional injury, such as feelings of harassment or distress, not amounting to psychiatric or mental injury, constitutes injury?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is on compensation orders for victims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 359 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the Court is required, after the conviction of an accused, to consider whether or not to make an order for the accused to pay compensation to the person injured.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This gives due regard to the harm suffered by the victim of a crime who is an equal participant in the criminal justice system and not simply a means to an end of convicting the accused.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is also an important mechanism to provide some measure of compensation for the victim of a crime, without requiring the victim to commence lengthy and costly civil proceedings separately after criminal proceedings conclude.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Shanmugam announced in his Ministerial Statement that the Ministry will be setting up a Sentencing Advisory Panel to issue non-binding sentencing guidelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister also consider including in the Panel’s scope of work a review and publication of guidelines on compensation quantum under section 359 of the Criminal Procedure Code?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome these amendments to provide greater protection to the most vulnerable groups of our society – children and foreign domestic workers, or FDWs, included.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, these amendments also enhance the punishment for sexual offences and violence against such groups.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I agree with the strong signal that abuse of vulnerable persons, children and FDWs cannot be condoned.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The current amendments also expand the jurisdiction of the District Court and Magistrates' Court to hear and mete out enhanced punishments for racially or religiously aggravated offences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a welcomed move, especially given the recent discussions on race and racism issues.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that these amendments, together with the introduction of the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act in the future, shall help promote and preserve our racial and religious harmony which is precious to all of us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps a harsher sentence or appropriate restitution or compensation order should be made in that respect.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, I welcome the enhanced penalties under the amendment to section 354(1) of the Penal Code, which increases the penalty for the outrage of modesty cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is the rationale for not increasing the penalty under section 354(2), if I may ask?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously, the offence, if committed against children, attracts more than double the punishment, if not committed against children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why not cover all minors under 16 years old?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be consistent with the offences of sexual grooming or exploitation in sections 376A to 376EE.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In summary, Mr Speaker, Sir, I welcome the amendments to enhance the punishment for sexual offences and violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think there needs to be greater protection for not only children under 14 years of age but all minors under 16 years old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will deal with the questions and suggestions raised by Members in turn.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got to take reference from other penalties across different sections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether the age limit for caning remains fit for our purpose today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The number of men over the age of 50 arrested for serious offences that attract caning is significantly lower, compared to men under the age of 50.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member raised the concern of offenders who are near the age of 50 delaying the proceedings to escape caning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Raising the age limit, by itself, may not stop the problem because, when you shift the line, the problem may also shift.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I accept that, in logical terms, by reference to life expectancy, Mr Murali Pillai's case is a cogent one.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My response to him is that we have been quite cautious about extending the categories of people who are caned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the example cited by Mr Murali Pillai of the accused person who tried to delay proceedings, caning was not carried out in that case because the accused was found medically unfit for caning, not because he had crossed the age of 50.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court then imposed an additional imprisonment term of 12 months, on top of the initial imprisonment sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the Sentencing Advisory Panel as well and whether it could review and publish guidelines on victim compensation under section 359 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Compensation orders under the CPC are meant for cases where the fact and the extent of damage are either agreed or readily and easily ascertainable on the evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas sought clarification on the rationale for amending section 182.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim made the point as to whether the amendment is necessary, considering that giving false information to a public servant is already dealt with by section 177.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas pointed out, section 177 applies if the person giving false information was legally bound to provide the information to a public servant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Chua Wen Hao's case, again, as both Members of Parliament pointed out, the Court said that section 182 is not designed to protect a public servant from the inefficient exercise of lawful powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, I should make clear that inefficient exercise in that case arose from false information being given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because false information was given, the Police had to spend extra time running around, doing the investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court held that an offence under section 182 was not made out although Police took more time to investigate the identity of one of the persons of interest because the Police would have had to investigate this case anyway, regardless of the false information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are amending section 182 in a very simple way to deal with this lacuna.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 182 applies even when you give false information even though you are not under an obligation to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 177 applies when the person is under a legal obligation to give information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I note Ms Sylvia Lim's point on the marginal note.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We did not amend the marginal note of the provision because the main thrust of the offence has not changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The intent and the scope of the amendment, of course, is made clear through the wording of the provision, the illustration that has been added, the Explanatory Statement and the discussion in the House today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim highlighted the overlaps between sections 177 and 186, and sought clarification on the rationale for raising the maximum imprisonment term for section 186, even though providing false information to a public servant when one is under a legal duty to do so, which is section 177, is arguably more serious than when one is not under such a duty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On section 186, I think Ms Sylvia Lim is right if both cases involve giving of false information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sections 177 and 186, however, can cover different types of criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 177, as we have just seen earlier, applies when one is under a legal duty to give information to a public servant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The provision of the false information is the central element of the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In contrast, section 186 deals with obstruction of public servants in the discharge of their public functions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can be through the provision of false information but it can also be through other means and one can imagine easily very egregious circumstances – deliberate physical obstruction of public servants when they are doing something extremely important and urgent, for example, in the saving of lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Quite apart from giving of false information, the crux of the offence under section 186, therefore, is, in some way, interfering or obstructing the performance of a public servant's duties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The new illustration being added will help to explain this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the illustration: a person plays a prank on, say, SCDF paramedics who are responding to an emergency and he gives false information to the paramedics with an intention of causing a delay in the paramedics' provision of medical assistance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even though the person may not be legally bound to provide information, his act of giving false information, intentionally wasting SCDF's time and resources in the midst of an emergency, could lead to very serious, possibly even fatal consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the proposed amendments clarify that section 186 is not limited to physical acts of obstruction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They could also include the provision of false information, depending on the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the essence of the offences is distinct and primarily addresses different types of conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The actual penalty imposed will, of course, depend on the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas also highlighted the overlaps between section 177 and the amended section 182 and asked if accused persons will be charged under section 182 instead of the less serious section 177.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is up to the prosecution to assess, exercising their prosecutorial discretion, as to which offence has been established, which charge should be preferred, depending on the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim suggested that persons who obstruct public servants in the discharge of their public functions under section 186 should face a jail term of up to two years, compared to the six months proposed in this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has said that obstruction could lead to grave consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree that it could lead to grave consequences, but, at present, having reviewed it, we do not see a need to increase the maximum sentence, based on the cases that have arisen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the more egregious instances raised by the Member will likely be caught by more serious offences, such as section 353 on using criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging his duty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third area is the protection of minors from sexual offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked why aggravated penalties for outrage of modesty under section 354(2) only apply when the minor is under 14 years old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He suggested aggravated penalty should also apply when a minor is under 16, consistent with the offences of sexual grooming and exploitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This question was considered by the Penal Code Review Committee (PCRC).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Both sets of offences – whether the victim is below 16 or below 14 – are treated seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The criterion of 14 years of age under section 354(2) is consistent with this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Sharael Taha expressed concern about sexual grooming in the digital space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He asked three questions: first, whether the offence of sexual grooming will cover persons who send links to sexual images or content through various online platforms; second, whether the Government could consider setting up a platform for members of the public to report such perpetrators; and third, how will the Government act on information if the perpetrators are not within Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2019, we amended the Penal Code to introduce specific offences relating to technology-facilitated sexual offending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These offences include sexual communications with minors, sexual activity or image in the presence of a minor and depending on the facts of the case, the act of sending links to sexual images or content to a minor under the age of 16 will be covered by this rubric of offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A similar situation will apply if the minor is aged between 16 and 18, and the perpetrator is in an exploitative relationship with the minor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But bringing him into Singapore and making him face justice is, of course, a separate question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The offences will also apply, regardless of the online platform through which the sexual content was communicated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this will cover links sent via Instagram, WhatsApp, TikTok, games platforms and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parents and other persons who wish to report such incidents can lodge a Police report online or in person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In investigating these crimes, the Police will identify the available evidence, including digital evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police will also work with external stakeholders by requesting information from online platforms, including message applications, or from telecommunication companies to try and identify the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where the perpetrator is not in Singapore, the Police work with foreign law enforcement agencies to investigate such cases within the ambit of existing international agreements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fourth area relates to the Government's measures to rehabilitate the offender and protect the public, especially vulnerable members of the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng sought clarification on the counselling and treatment provided to persons who committed hurt and sexual offences and whether we can consider mandating post-release treatment for these offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked if the Government could consider a registry to prevent convicted sexual offenders from working with vulnerable individuals, such as children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also asked about digital deterrence and whether the Government could monitor the online activities of sexual offenders who had preyed on victims online after they had served their sentences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates undergo various rehabilitative programmes while in prison and also post-release, if needed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During incarceration, inmates will be placed on programmes which are calibrated based on their general risks of reoffending and rehabilitation needs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These programmes include psychology-based correctional programmes, family programmes, employability skills training and religious programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If assessed suitable, eligible inmates may be emplaced on community-based programmes towards the tail-end of their incarceration to continue their rehabilitation in the community under supervision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inmates who had committed sexual offences may be referred to community partners before their release if they are assessed to require longer-term support for their successful rehabilitation and reintegration into the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The CRS seeks to deter ex-offenders from reoffending by subjecting them to conditions upon their release.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If an ex-offender breaches the basic condition of not committing another offence under the CRS and is sentenced to imprisonment, the Court may impose an enhanced sentence as a penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This includes ex-offenders who had committed certain sexual offences, such as rape and sexual penetration of a minor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the MAS, released offenders undergo close supervision under the Singapore Prson Service (SPS) and have to comply with the mandatory aftercare conditions imposed by the Commissioner of Prisons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such conditions may include attending counselling or therapy, regular reporting and wearing of electronic monitoring devices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the supervisee breaches his supervision conditions, he will be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he commits new criminal offences, he may be charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supervisees also undergo counselling and case management for up to two years, to help them in their rehabilitation and reintegration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supervisees who had committed sexual offences will continue to receive counselling support from SPS's Correctional Rehabilitation Specialists, if required.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the suggestion to monitor the online activities of sexual offenders after their release, there are practical limitations on how this can be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some overseas jurisdictions which implemented such restrictions faced manpower challenges to track online activities for an extended period of time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Additionally, as Members will appreciate, measures to control such activities can easily be bypassed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for preventing convicted sex offenders from working with vulnerable people like children by setting up a sex offenders' registry, I mentioned this to the House in April this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police already maintains a non-public record of persons convicted of serious offences, including sexual offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some practical difficulties with this approach, which we are carefully considering.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fifth area is the protection for persons accused of crimes, especially those accused of sexual offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about protecting the identity of persons accused of sexual crimes before conviction and he referred to what I said in May this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are pros and cons for both approaches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our current approach is towards open Court proceedings and I had said that it is not set in stone and we will keep the position under review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as of today, as of now, the current position is open Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And while you can cite individual cases, overall, the question is: what helps in advancing, in maintaining rule of law and the justice system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Sharael Taha commented that the criminal justice system should not be abused by persons who lodge false reports out of spite or mischief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We agree and it is an offence to make false allegations in Court, or lodge false Police reports.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Persons who are convicted of making false reports could face severe penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked if our amendments to the provisions on Mistake or Ignorance of Fact under section 79, or Mistake or Ignorance of Law under section 79A and Accident in the doing of a Lawful Act under section 80, operate to shift the burden of proof and whether there are safeguards to prevent the accused from abusing these provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These amendments are not meant to change the general principles on burden of proof.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Suppose the accused is charged with theft of a watch, the offence of theft has the fault element of dishonesty, which the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt and I do not think there is any question on that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Suppose the accused claims a mistake of fact that he mistakenly believed that the watch was his, he needs to show that to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Overall, after taking into account the different facts and different parties in a case may have the burden of proving specific facts, the Prosecution has to show to the Court that the accused had acted dishonestly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke on the defence of unsoundness of mind under section 84 and suggested for the defence to be broadened in two ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this was covered in the 2019 Penal Code amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are quite cautious about further expanding the defence to cover persons whose mental disorder impaired their control over their actions, but who retained some control over their actions despite their mental disorder.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In principle, a person who retains some power to control his actions, but does not do so, remains blameworthy and should face the appropriate legal consequences as opposed to a full acquittal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai also suggested that section 84(b) be amended to apply disjunctively, instead of conjunctively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other words, to be acquitted under this defence, the accused person needs only to show either that he was incapable of knowing that what he was doing was wrong by the ordinary standards of reasonable and honest persons, or that he was incapable of knowing that it was wrong as contrary to the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We considered this issue during the last review of the Penal Code in 2019.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just because a person was incapable of knowing that his action was contrary to law does not mean that we should avail the defence to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai said that an acquittal due to the defence of unsoundness of mind would be a Pyrrhic victory, as the accused will be ordered by the Minister to be kept in safe custody, which usually means a psychiatric institution "during the President's pleasure".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reasons why that is done is that if he is released out, the person may go out and do more harm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there is also a significance to a conviction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a finding that a person is guilty and should be appropriately punished.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are not narrowing the ambit of the defence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During imprisonment, prisoners with serious mental disorders receive treatment by professionals from both the Prisons and the Institute of Mental Health, or IMH.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When prisoners are due to be released, those whose conditions remain severe enough to warrant immediate follow-up are assessed directly by IMH.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMH may decide to detain the individuals further at IMH under the provisions of the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: IMH can act in those ways and the Act allows for the detention of a person at IMH for treatment if he is suffering from a mental disorder which warrants his detention at IMH for treatment; and it is in the interests of the health or safety of the person or for the protection of other persons, that he should be detained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In less severe cases, Prisons may make referrals to IMH or polyclinics for follow-up care, after the offender's release from prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But ultimately, this relates to public safety and protection, which is a separate issue from that of criminal responsibility, which is what section 84 is basically concerned with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai cited the case of Public Prosecutor v Dolah Bin Omar, to suggest that the defence of unsoundness of mind should be broadened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that case, the unsoundness of mind defence was not pleaded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lawyer for the accused and the Judge both accepted that on the evidence, the accused's mental condition did not come within the rubric of unsoundness of mind defence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is nothing to indicate that the accused would have qualified for the defence, regardless of whether a disjunctive or conjunctive reading is to be applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Thomas suggested including a definition or illustrations to make clear what "genital region" refers to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The term "genital region" is currently used in existing provisions to define child abuse material and there have not been concerns raised over the interpretation of this term so far.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is a fair degree of clarity on it and we do not expect that there will be difficulty in interpreting the term in the context of the offence of voyeurism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if such difficulties arise, we will relook at this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng sought clarifications on our proposals to update older terms in the Penal Code, say, replacing the word "malice" with the phrase with "intent to cause injury".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To clarify, the phrase "intent to cause injury" relates or refers to the offender's mental state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, an offender may be found to have intended to cause injury, even if he had not succeeded in causing the specific type of injury intended or injuring the intended victim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As stated in the definition of "injury", any harm that is illegally caused to the victim, in the mind, will amount to an injury.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not necessary for the harm to take the form of a psychiatric or mental disorder, for there to be an injury.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will have to decide in each case, based on the circumstances, whether there is harm that is illegally caused to the victim's mind.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Feelings of harassment or distress may, depending on the circumstances, satisfy this test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain sought clarification on who section 304C targets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Members will realise, a child under 14 years old as well as a domestic worker can broadly be classified as vulnerable persons as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Frequently, we have come across cases, child, five years old or six years old, scalded, beaten up, bones broken, brought to the hospital, dead and some story is given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, it is very difficult to prove in Court who committed the abuse and who permitted the abuse.
